overview.description: HTTP is the protocol of the web: a client asks for a resource, such as an HTML page, and the server answers with a status code, headers and usually a body. Every exchange is one request and one response, written as readable text in HTTP/1.1.

outro.title: Page delivered
outro.text: In under a tenth of a second the laptop looked up an address, opened a TCP connection and exchanged one HTTP request and response, all of it readable by anyone on the path. Press REPLAY to watch it again.

steps.title: Client Request
steps.detail: You open https://ssp-academy.com/. The browser will send a GET request, but packets travel to IP addresses, not names, so first it needs the server’s address. (Browsers now try https:// first; this is the plain version.)

steps.title: DNS Resolution
steps.detail: The laptop asks the DNS server it was given by DHCP, 8.8.8.8, for the address of https://ssp-academy.com/. The query goes over UDP port 53 and the answer is an A record with the IPv4 address. (On a network with IPv6 it would also ask for an AAAA record.)

steps.title: Page Rendering
steps.detail: The browser parses the HTML and paints the page. Linked CSS, images and scripts would each start more requests just like this one, reusing the open connection where they can.

overview.description: HTTPS is HTTP sent through an encrypted TLS connection. TLS proves the server is who it claims to be with a certificate, agrees on fresh encryption keys, and then protects every request and response from being read or changed on the way.

outro.title: Secure page delivered
outro.text: The browser looked up the address in plain DNS, opened a TCP connection, checked the server’s certificate and agreed on keys in one round trip. Every HTTP byte after that travelled encrypted. Press REPLAY to watch it again.

steps.title: Secure Request
steps.detail: You type https://ssp-academy.com/. The “s” tells the browser to protect the connection with TLS, on port 443 by default. Before it can connect at all, it still has to find the server’s IP address.

steps.title: DNS Lookup
steps.desc: Same lookup as HTTP, not encrypted
steps.detail: The lookup is exactly the same as for plain HTTP: a query to 8.8.8.8 over UDP port 53. It is not encrypted, so anyone on the path can see which name you asked for, unless the browser uses DNS over HTTPS.

steps.title: Page Rendering
steps.detail: The browser decrypts the response, paints the page and shows a padlock: the connection is private and the server proved its identity. The Strict-Transport-Security header tells it to use HTTPS for this site from now on.

overview.description: TCP turns the internet’s best-effort packet delivery into a reliable, ordered stream of bytes. It numbers every byte, acknowledges what arrives, resends what goes missing, and paces the sender so neither the other side nor the network is overwhelmed.

outro.title: Connection closed
outro.text: TCP opened a connection, numbered and acknowledged every byte, spotted a gap and resent just the missing segment, then closed both directions cleanly. curl received every byte in order and never saw the loss. Press REPLAY to watch it again.

steps.title: Open Connection
steps.detail: curl already knows the server’s address. Before any data moves, both sides choose a starting sequence number and confirm it: SYN, SYN-ACK, ACK. The numbers here are relative; real ones start at a random value.

overview.description: UDP sends data in independent packets called datagrams, with no connection, no acknowledgements and no resends. That keeps it fast and light: right for voice, video, games and DNS, where a late answer is worse than a missing one.

outro.title: Call keeps flowing
outro.text: Audio started with the very first packet, every datagram travelled on its own, and the one that was lost was simply gone: UDP never noticed. The app covered the gap and the call carried on. Press REPLAY to watch it again.

steps.title: The App Decides
steps.desc: Reliability is up to the app
steps.detail: The call app numbers its own frames (RTP does this), so it sees that frame 7 is missing and smooths over the 20 ms gap instead of waiting. Waiting for a resend would make the whole call lag.

overview.description: IP gives every device an address and moves packets from network to network. Each router looks only at the destination address to choose the next hop. IP is best effort: it doesn’t promise delivery or order. TCP adds those on top.

outro.title: There and back
outro.text: The laptop sent the packet to its router, which swapped in its public address. Twelve routers in all passed it along by destination address alone, and the reply found its way back the same way. Press REPLAY to watch it again.

steps.title: Local or Not?
steps.desc: Compare the address with the subnet
steps.detail: The laptop is 192.168.1.10 with a /24 mask, so its own network is 192.168.1.0 to 192.168.1.255. The server, 203.0.113.10, is outside that range, so the packet has to go to the default gateway: the home router.

steps.title: Find the Router
steps.desc: ARP turns an IP into a MAC
steps.detail: On the local network, frames are delivered by MAC address. If the router’s MAC isn’t in the laptop’s ARP cache, it broadcasts “who has 192.168.1.1?” and the router answers with its MAC address.

overview.description: DNS turns names like https://ssp-academy.com/ into the IP addresses computers use to reach each other. No single server knows every name: the system is a hierarchy of servers, and answers are cached along the way so most lookups never have to go far.

outro.title: Name resolved
outro.text: Starting from an empty cache, the resolver walked from the root to .com to example.com’s own server, then answered the laptop. Until the TTL runs out, the next lookup for this name is answered straight from a cache. Press REPLAY to watch it again.

overview.description: DHCP hands a device everything it needs to use a network: an IP address, the subnet mask, the router to send traffic through and the DNS servers to ask. Addresses are leased for a set time and renewed while the device stays on the network.

outro.title: On the network
outro.desc: Leased, and kept up to date
outro.text: Four messages took the laptop from no address to a working configuration, and halfway through the 24-hour lease it renewed it with a direct request to the router. Press REPLAY to watch it again.

steps.title: No Address Yet
steps.detail: The laptop has just connected. It has a MAC address built in, but no IP address, no gateway and no DNS server, so it can’t talk to anything beyond its own network yet. It asks for them with DHCP.

steps.title: Discover
steps.detail: Without an address of its own, the laptop sends from 0.0.0.0 to the broadcast address 255.255.255.255, so every device on the local network receives it. Only DHCP servers answer.

overview.description: ICMP is how the network reports back: a router says a packet’s time ran out, a server says nothing is listening on a port. Tools like ping and traceroute are built from these messages. It travels inside IP but carries no application data.

outro.title: The network answered
outro.text: An echo request measured the round trip, packets with a small TTL made each router on the path identify itself, and a closed port was reported straight back. Press REPLAY to watch it again.

steps.title: Ping
steps.detail: “ping -n 1 203.0.113.10” sends one ICMP echo request (plain ping sends four, a second apart): type 8, code 0, with an identifier, a sequence number and 32 bytes of filler. The server’s system answers by itself, no application needed.

overview.description: SMTP moves email: from your mail app to your provider’s server, and from that server to the recipient’s. It is a conversation of short text commands, each answered with a three-digit reply code. Reading mail is a different job, done with IMAP or POP3.

outro.title: Mail delivered
outro.text: Mohamed’s app handed the message to her provider over an encrypted, logged-in connection. The provider found Bob’s mail server in DNS and relayed it there, upgrading that link to TLS. It now waits in Bob’s mailbox until he reads it with IMAP or POP3.

steps.title: Connect Securely
steps.detail: Mohamed presses Send. Her mail app connects to her provider’s submission server, smtp.example.com, on port 465. On this port TLS starts immediately, so the whole SMTP conversation, including her password, is encrypted.

steps.detail: With TLS on, the provider repeats EHLO, then the envelope and the message, now with a DKIM signature and a Received header added. Bob’s server checks SPF, DKIM and DMARC and accepts it.

overview.description: POP3 lets a mail app download messages from a mailbox on a server. It was designed for one device that fetches mail and then removes it from the server. Commands are short words, and every reply starts with +OK or -ERR.

outro.title: Mail downloaded
outro.text: Bob’s app logged in, saw two messages, downloaded the first and deleted it, which the server carried out at QUIT. That message now lives only on this laptop, which is why POP3 suits one device and IMAP suits several.

steps.title: Connect Securely
steps.detail: Bob’s mail app connects to pop.example.org on port 995, where TLS starts right away. Inside it, the server greets with +OK. (On port 110 the session starts in plain text and is upgraded with the STLS command.)

overview.description: IMAP lets mail apps work with a mailbox that stays on the server. Folders, read and flagged marks and deletions are kept there, so a phone, a laptop and webmail all see the same mailbox. The server can also tell an app about new mail as it arrives.

outro.title: Mailbox in sync
outro.text: Bob’s app opened his inbox, read a message, which marked it \Seen on the server for all his devices, and then waited with IDLE until the server announced new mail. Nothing was deleted: the server still holds everything.

steps.title: Connect Securely
steps.detail: Bob’s app connects to imap.example.org on port 993, where TLS starts right away. The server greets with an untagged “* OK” line that also lists its capabilities, such as IDLE.

steps.title: Log In

overview.description: FTP moves files between a client and a server. It is unusual in using two TCP connections: one for commands and replies, and a fresh one for each file or listing. It dates from the early 1970s and sends everything, passwords included, as plain text.

outro.title: File downloaded
outro.text: Commands went over the control connection, the file over its own data connection, and closing that connection marked the end of the file. Anyone on the path could have read the password and the file, which is why SFTP or FTPS is used today.

steps.title: Control Connection
steps.detail: The FTP app opens a TCP connection to ftp.example.com on port 21. This control connection carries commands and replies for the whole session. The server greets with 220. Like SMTP, every reply starts with a three-digit code.

steps.title: Log In
steps.desc: USER and PASS, readable by anyone
steps.detail: The app sends USER, the server asks for the password with 331, and PASS sends it. Nothing is encrypted, so the user name and password cross every network on the way as readable text.

steps.title: Passive Mode
steps.desc: The server names a data port
steps.detail: TYPE I asks for a byte-for-byte binary copy. PASV asks the server to open a port for the data connection. The reply encodes the address and port as six numbers: 195 × 256 + 149 = port 50069. The laptop connects out, which works through NAT.

overview.description: SSH gives you an encrypted, authenticated connection to another computer, to run commands on it, copy files (SFTP, scp) or carry other connections. The server proves who it is with a host key; you prove who you are with a key pair or a password.

outro.title: Logged in securely
outro.desc: Encrypted from the key exchange on
outro.text: The two sides agreed on algorithms, built shared keys with a post-quantum hybrid exchange, and the server proved its identity with its host key. Mohamed proved hers by signing with a private key that never left the laptop, then typed a command, one packet per key.

steps.title: Say Hello
steps.detail: Mohamed runs “ssh mohamed@server.example.com”. After the TCP handshake on port 22, each side sends one line of plain text naming the SSH protocol version (2.0) and its software. Everything else in SSH is binary.

overview.description: TLS puts a secure channel on top of TCP. It proves the server’s identity with a certificate, agrees on fresh keys, then encrypts and authenticates everything sent. HTTPS, secure email and many other protocols run inside it. SSL was the name of its predecessor.

outro.title: Secure from start to finish
outro.desc: One round trip to set up
outro.text: One round trip agreed on a version, a cipher and a post-quantum hybrid key. The certificate chain proved who the server was, and every byte after the Server Hello was encrypted and authenticated, right up to the close_notify. Press REPLAY to watch it again.

steps.title: Client Hello
steps.detail: After the TCP handshake the browser lists what it can do: TLS versions, cipher suites, and key shares for the groups it expects, including the post-quantum hybrid X25519MLKEM768. It also names the site (SNI) and the protocols it speaks (ALPN).

overview.description: A WebSocket keeps one connection open between a web page and a server, so either side can send a message at any moment: chat, live scores, games, shared documents. It starts as an ordinary HTTP request asking to upgrade; after that, messages travel in small frames with a header of just a few bytes.

outro.title: Connection closed
outro.text: One HTTP request turned an ordinary TCP connection into a two-way channel. After that every message cost a few bytes of header, and the server could send whenever it had something to say. Press REPLAY to watch it again.

steps.title: TCP Connection
steps.desc: TCP to the server, as for HTTP
steps.detail: The chat page is already open, loaded from https://ssp-academy.com/. Its script calls new WebSocket("ws://https://ssp-academy.com/chat"), and the browser starts with an ordinary TCP connection to port 80. (Real sites use wss://, the same thing inside TLS; plain ws:// lets you read every byte.)

steps.title: Switch Protocols
steps.detail: The server answers 101 Switching Protocols. Its Sec-WebSocket-Accept is the key with a fixed string added, hashed with SHA-1 and written in base64: proof that it understood the request. It didn’t take up compression, so messages go as plain text. HTTP is finished on this connection; from now on both sides send WebSocket frames.

steps.title: Live Updates
steps.detail: You send "Hello": a 2-byte header, a 4-byte masking key and the 5 masked bytes, 11 bytes in all instead of a whole HTTP request. Seconds later the server pushes Bob’s message without being asked: the connection is still open, so it can. Frames from the browser are always masked; frames from the server never are.

overview.description: Wi-Fi carries a network over radio. Before a device can send anything, it has to find the network, join it and prove it knows the password. With WPA2-Personal that proof is the 4-way handshake: four short messages that turn the password into fresh encryption keys, without the password ever going over the air.

outro.title: Connected
outro.desc: Eleven frames to a secure link
outro.text: The laptop found the network, joined it with two formalities and proved it knew the password in a four-message handshake, without ever sending it. Everything after that was encrypted with keys made for this connection alone. Press REPLAY to watch it again.

steps.title: Find the Network
steps.detail: About ten times a second the router’s Wi-Fi sends a beacon: here is "HomeNet", protected with WPA2, on channel 36. The laptop could simply wait to hear one; to be quicker it also asks out loud with a probe request, and the access point answers with a probe response.

fields.note: Nobody acknowledges a broadcast, so nothing is booked.

fields.name: Capabilities
fields.note: Privacy bit set: joining takes a key.

fields.name: RSN

fields.name: Group cipher
fields.note: Encrypts broadcasts, which every device on the network can read.

fields.name: Pairwise cipher
fields.note: Encrypts each device’s own traffic, with keys only it and the access point have.

fields.note: Wi-Fi 4, 5 and 6 capabilities and settings (HT, VHT, HE: channel 36, 80 MHz wide), and vendor extras.

steps.title: Encrypted Now
steps.desc: And what a listener could still do
steps.detail: Every data frame is encrypted now, like this first one carrying a DHCP Discover: anyone nearby sees only the MAC addresses and the size. But someone who recorded the four handshake messages can try password guesses at home, as fast as their computer allows: a guess is right when it gives the same MIC. A long, random password makes that hopeless; WPA3 removes the weakness.

overview.description: WPA3 is the current Wi-Fi security standard. Its Personal mode keeps the simple shared password but changes how it is checked: SAE, a password exchange that no recording can attack offline, gives every connection a fresh key. It also makes protected management frames compulsory.

outro.title: Connected with WPA3
outro.text: The laptop and the access point proved to each other that they know the password without giving anyone a way to test guesses offline, then made fresh keys exactly as WPA2 does. Press REPLAY to watch it again.

steps.title: Why It’s Safer
steps.detail: With WPA2, anyone in range could forge a “disconnect” frame and knock a device off the network, often to record its handshake when it joined again. WPA3 requires protected management frames, so forged disconnects are ignored. Many routers also offer a transition mode that lets WPA2 devices join too; those devices keep WPA2’s weaknesses.

overview.description: Hotels, cafés, airports and trains often put a login page in front of their Wi-Fi. Until you accept the terms (or pay), the router lets nothing out to the internet. It catches your device’s first plain HTTP request and answers it with a redirect to its own page; your device notices because a test page it knows comes back wrong.

outro.title: Online
outro.text: Windows asked a test page for an answer it knows and got a redirect instead, so it knew a portal was in the way and opened the login page. Once the terms were accepted, the router let the laptop through, and the same check came back right. Press REPLAY to watch it again.

steps.title: Joined, Offline
steps.desc: An address, but no way out
steps.detail: The laptop has joined the hotel’s Wi-Fi, which has no password, and got an address from the router by DHCP. The router answers the laptop itself and passes on its DNS lookups, but drops anything else bound for the internet until the guest has logged in. (An open network also means anyone nearby can read whatever isn’t protected by HTTPS.)

steps.title: Internet Check
steps.detail: After joining any network, Windows looks up www.msftconnecttest.com (the router passes the lookup on) and asks it for /connecttest.txt over plain HTTP; the right answer is the text "Microsoft Connect Test". The router catches the connection and answers the handshake itself, in the test server’s name. The laptop can’t tell yet.

steps.title: Redirected
steps.desc: The wrong answer gives it away
steps.detail: Instead of the test text, the "server" answers 302 Found, pointing to the router’s login page. Its TTL is 64, not lowered at all, because it came straight from the router. Windows sees the wrong answer, marks the network as needing action and opens the browser, whose first request the router redirects the same way, to its login page. This only works with plain HTTP: the router can’t fake an HTTPS page without a certificate error.

overview.full: Forward proxy, and CONNECT for HTTPS
overview.description: A forward proxy fetches web pages on your behalf. Companies and schools use one to filter sites, keep copies of popular pages and log what goes out; the sites you visit see the proxy, not you. Plain HTTP passes through it in the clear. For HTTPS the browser asks the proxy for a tunnel, and the encrypted connection runs through it unread.

outro.title: Two ways through
outro.text: For the plain page, the proxy did the work: it read the request, fetched the page on its own connection and could have kept, changed or refused it. For HTTPS it only opened a tunnel and copied encrypted bytes, knowing nothing but the site’s name. Press REPLAY to watch it again.

steps.title: Proxy Settings
steps.detail: The browser is set to send everything through a proxy at 192.0.2.80, port 8080, as many companies and schools require. You open https://ssp-academy.com/. The browser doesn’t look up https://ssp-academy.com/ itself: it connects to the proxy and leaves the rest to it.

steps.title: To the Proxy
steps.detail: The laptop opens an ordinary TCP connection, not to the website, but to the proxy’s port 8080.

steps.title: In the Tunnel
steps.detail: From now on the proxy copies bytes both ways without reading them. The browser’s TLS Client Hello goes in on the laptop’s connection and comes out, byte for byte the same, on the proxy’s connection to the server. TLS runs from end to end, so the proxy learns the site’s name and the sizes, never the pages. (Some company proxies do open HTTPS, using a certificate authority installed on every company laptop; then they see everything.)

overview.description: SOCKS is a general-purpose proxy. Where an HTTP proxy understands web requests, a SOCKS proxy simply opens a connection on your behalf and copies the bytes, whatever the protocol: web, email, games, SSH. Apps use it to reach a network through one gateway, or to hide their own address; ssh -D and Tor both offer one.

outro.title: Tunnel open
outro.desc: A few bytes, then just copying
outro.text: Four tiny messages told the proxy where to connect; after that it only copied bytes. The website saw the proxy’s address, and because the laptop sent a name rather than an address, even the DNS lookup happened at the proxy. Press REPLAY to watch it again.

steps.title: To the Proxy
steps.detail: An app set to use a SOCKS proxy (a browser, a game launcher, or a tunnel made with ssh -D) opens a TCP connection to it, port 1080. SOCKS doesn’t care what will travel inside: it can carry any TCP connection.

steps.title: Greeting
steps.desc: Version 5, and how to log in
steps.detail: The laptop sends three bytes: version 5, one login method offered, and that method, 0: no login. The proxy answers with two: version 5, method 0. Had it chosen method 2, the app would next send a user name and password, in plain text.

overview.description: A reverse proxy stands in front of a website’s servers: visitors connect to it, and it passes their requests on to an app server behind it. It can spread the load over many servers, keep copies of pages and turn away attacks. Often it also does the TLS work, decrypting HTTPS at the edge so the servers behind it speak plain HTTP. That is SSL (or TLS) offloading.

outro.title: Served from the edge
outro.text: The laptop saw one HTTPS website. Behind it, the reverse proxy decrypted the request, asked an app server in plain HTTP over the private network and encrypted the answer for the trip back. Press REPLAY to watch it again.

steps.title: The Front Door
steps.detail: The laptop opens https://ssp-academy.com/. The address DNS gives for the name belongs to the reverse proxy, which holds the site’s certificate and does the TLS handshake. Nothing tells the laptop there is another server behind it.

steps.title: TLS Ends Here
steps.desc: Offloading: the proxy does the TLS work
steps.detail: The request arrives encrypted, and the reverse proxy decrypts it. That is the offloading: the TLS work is done here, once, instead of on every app server. Now the proxy can read the URL, headers and cookies, and pick a server by them.

steps.title: In the Clear
steps.desc: Passed on to the app server
steps.detail: The proxy passes the request on over the data centre’s private network, as plain HTTP to port 8080. It adds X-Forwarded-For, the visitor’s address, and X-Forwarded-Proto: https, how the visitor came in; otherwise the app would see only the proxy. Anyone able to watch this private network could read it all.

steps.title: Three Options
steps.detail: Offloading, as here, is simple and fast but leaves the inside traffic readable. Re-encrypting opens a second TLS connection from the proxy to the app server, so it stays encrypted inside too. Passing through forwards the TLS bytes without opening them: the certificate lives on the app servers, and the proxy can only choose a server by address and the name in the Client Hello, not by URL.

overview.description: A VPN carries your traffic inside an encrypted tunnel to a VPN server, which sends it on to the internet. On a café’s Wi-Fi, others see only encrypted packets going to the VPN server; websites see the VPN server’s address instead of yours. WireGuard is a modern VPN: a small amount of code, one fixed set of modern algorithms and a handshake of two messages.

outro.title: Tunnel up
outro.desc: Encrypted to the VPN, plain beyond it
outro.text: Two handshake messages made the keys. After that every packet the laptop sent was sealed whole inside a UDP packet to the VPN server, and the website saw only the VPN server’s address. Beyond the VPN server traffic is no better protected than without one, so HTTPS still matters. Press REPLAY to watch it again.

steps.title: Set Up Once
steps.detail: The laptop runs the WireGuard app with a short configuration: its own private key, the server’s public key and address (192.0.2.51, UDP port 51820), and AllowedIPs = 0.0.0.0/0, which means everything goes through the tunnel. Inside the tunnel the laptop’s address is 10.8.0.2.

steps.title: Handshake
steps.detail: When the laptop first has something to send, it starts a handshake: 148 bytes with a fresh public key, its own long-term key (encrypted, so only the server learns who is calling) and the time (encrypted, so a recording can’t be replayed). The server answers only keys it knows, here with 92 bytes. One round trip, and both sides have new session keys.

steps.title: Out to the Web
steps.detail: The VPN server decrypts the packet, swaps 10.8.0.2 for its own public address (NAT) and sends the SYN on, one hop older (TTL 127). The SYN offers a maximum segment of 1380 bytes, not 1460: the tunnel adds 60 bytes to every packet. The web server sees a visitor at 192.0.2.51 and answers there.

steps.title: Keeping It Open
steps.detail: With nothing to send, a WireGuard tunnel goes quiet. Because the laptop is behind NAT, it is set to send an empty packet every 25 seconds (PersistentKeepalive), a keepalive of 32 bytes, so the router doesn’t forget the connection. Every two minutes a new handshake makes fresh keys, and if the laptop moves to another network, the tunnel simply carries on from its new address.

overview.description: IPsec protects IP packets themselves. IKEv2 sets things up: the two sides agree on algorithms, make keys and prove who they are with certificates or other credentials. Then ESP carries each packet encrypted inside another. IPsec links offices together and brings laptops into company networks, and it is built into most operating systems and firewalls.

outro.title: Tunnel up
outro.desc: IKE to set up, ESP to carry
outro.text: Four IKE messages agreed on algorithms, found the NAT, proved both identities and set up the tunnel. After that each packet travelled whole inside ESP, encrypted and checked, and wrapped in UDP to get through the home router. Press REPLAY to watch it again.

steps.title: IKE_SA_INIT
steps.detail: The VPN client opens with IKE on UDP port 500. Its first message proposes the algorithms (AES-GCM with 256-bit keys, SHA-256, Curve25519) and carries a public key and a random nonce; the gateway picks the proposal and sends its own key and nonce. Both now share a secret, but neither has proved who it is yet.

At the gateway they don’t match what arrived: the home router rewrote the laptop’s address on the way (NAT). steps.title: Which VPN?
steps.detail: IPsec is older and very flexible: it negotiates its algorithms, takes many kinds of credentials and is built into Windows, macOS, iOS, Android and most firewalls, which makes it the usual way to join a company network or link two offices. WireGuard does less, with far less code and one fixed set of algorithms.

overview.description: QUIC is a newer transport that runs over UDP and has TLS 1.3 built in. Its first packets do the transport and the encryption handshakes together, so a page request can leave after one round trip. It carries many streams at once, so one lost packet doesn’t hold up the rest, and it survives a change of network. HTTP/3 is HTTP running over QUIC.

outro.title: Page delivered
outro.desc: One round trip, then the request
outro.text: QUIC folded the transport and TLS handshakes into one round trip, so the request left 36 ms after the first packet; over TCP and TLS it would have waited twice as long. Everything after the first packets was encrypted, even most of each packet’s header. Press REPLAY to watch it again.

steps.title: Choosing HTTP/3
steps.desc: An earlier visit said it can
steps.detail: On an earlier visit the server answered with Alt-Svc: h3=":443", meaning it also speaks HTTP/3 on UDP port 443 (DNS can say the same in an HTTPS record). So this time the browser skips TCP and talks QUIC.

steps.title: Initial Packets
steps.detail: There is no separate TCP handshake: the very first packets carry the TLS Client Hello. With its post-quantum key share it is 1,880 bytes, too big for one packet, so it fills two Initial packets. Each datagram is padded to at least 1,200 bytes; a server may send back only three times what it has received, so a forged sender address can’t turn it into an amplifier.

steps.title: Finished + GET
steps.desc: The request, one round trip in
steps.detail: The laptop checks the certificate and sends its Finished, and in the same moment its first HTTP/3 request in a 1-RTT packet: a HEADERS frame on stream 0, its headers compressed with QPACK. One round trip after the first packet, the request is on its way; TCP and TLS together would need two.

steps.title: New Network
steps.desc: Known by ID, not by address
steps.detail: A QUIC connection is known by its connection IDs, not by addresses and ports. If the laptop moves from Wi-Fi to a phone’s hotspot, its address changes but the connection carries on: the server checks the new path and continues. And on the next visit the browser can send its request in its very first packets (0-RTT).

overview.description: IPv6 addresses are 128 bits long, enough for every device to have its own. A device can usually set itself up with no DHCP server: it makes a link-local address, asks for a router, and builds its global address from the prefix the router advertises (SLAAC). Neighbour discovery, part of ICMPv6, finds MAC addresses and does the work ARP does for IPv4.

outro.title: Two addresses, no DHCP
outro.text: The laptop made a link-local address and a global one, checked that nobody else had either, and learned its router, MTU and DNS server from a single advertisement. When packets came for it, neighbour discovery found its MAC address. Press REPLAY to watch it again.

steps.title: Link-Local First
steps.detail: Every IPv6 interface gets a link-local address, usable only on its own network. The laptop makes one from fe80:: and a random-looking 64-bit interface ID. First it checks nobody already has it: a Neighbor Solicitation asking for that address, sent from :: because it can’t use the address yet. Nobody answers, so it’s the laptop’s.

steps.desc: Prefix, MTU and DNS in one message
steps.detail: The router answers to ff02::1, every device on the network, with a Router Advertisement: use me as your way out for 30 minutes, here is my MAC address, the MTU is 1500, the network’s prefix is 2001:db8:1234:5678::/64 and you may make your own address in it, and ask 2001:4860:4860::8888 for DNS. Routers also send these on their own every few minutes.

steps.title: A Global Address
steps.detail: The laptop joins the prefix and its interface ID into a global address, 2001:db8:1234:5678:8d2e:4f61:a9b0:7c13, and checks it the same way. Windows also makes a temporary address with a random ID that changes every day, used for outgoing connections so websites can’t follow one device by its address.

steps.title: Neighbour Lookup
steps.detail: A reply from the internet arrives at the router for the laptop’s global address. To deliver it, the router needs the MAC address that goes with it: it sends a Neighbor Solicitation to the address’s solicited-node group, so only devices whose address ends the same way even look. The laptop answers with a Neighbor Advertisement carrying its MAC address.

steps.title: Ready, No DHCP
steps.detail: The laptop is on the internet with its own global address, and no NAT changes it on the way: the address a website sees is the laptop’s. The home router’s firewall still turns away connections nobody inside asked for. Networks that want to hand out addresses centrally can use DHCPv6 instead.

overview.description: Computer clocks drift by seconds a week, and a lot depends on them: certificates have dates, logins and payments expire, logs from different machines must line up. NTP sets a clock from a time server over the internet. One small request and answer carry four timestamps, enough to work out how far off the clock is and how long the network took.

outro.title: Clock set
outro.text: One request and one answer gave four timestamps. From them the laptop worked out that its clock was 0.25 s slow and that the network took 24 ms there and back, and it began easing its clock into line. Press REPLAY to watch it again.

steps.title: Clocks Drift
steps.desc: The laptop’s clock is a little slow
steps.detail: A computer keeps time with a quartz crystal that runs a little fast or slow, so clocks drift apart by seconds a week. This laptop’s clock is a quarter of a second behind. Windows sets it from time.windows.com, whose address it has already looked up by DNS.

steps.title: Ask for the Time
steps.detail: The laptop sends a 48-byte request to port 123. It writes in the time by its own clock as the request leaves: T1, 09:40:59.750. Everything else is empty.

steps.title: The Answer
steps.desc: T2 and T3 from the server, T4 on arrival
steps.detail: The server copies T1 back, adds T2, when the request arrived, and T3, when its answer leaves, both by its own accurate clock. When the answer arrives, the laptop notes T4 by its own clock. The server is stratum 2: it sets its clock from a stratum 1 server, which has a GPS receiver or an atomic clock.

steps.title: The Offset
steps.detail: The time on the network, there and back, is (T4 − T1) − (T3 − T2) = 24.0 ms. The offset assumes the trip takes as long each way: ((T2 − T1) + (T3 − T4)) / 2 = 250.0 ms. The laptop’s clock is a quarter of a second slow. An uneven route (slower one way than the other) would skew the result by up to half the difference.

steps.title: Ease It In
steps.detail: A small error is not fixed in one jump: the clock is run slightly fast until it catches up, so time never stops or goes backwards for running programs. Only a big error is set straight away. As a clock settles, an NTP client asks less often, from every 64 seconds up to every 17 minutes or so; Windows on its own checks time.windows.com far less often, every several hours or less.

overview.description: Ordinary DNS travels in the clear: anyone on the same Wi-Fi, and your internet provider, can read every name you look up and even change the answers. DNS over HTTPS (DoH) sends the same DNS messages inside an encrypted HTTPS connection to the resolver, so on the way they look like any other web traffic. Browsers and operating systems can turn it on.

outro.title: Looked up in private
outro.text: The plain lookup could be read by anyone on the path. Over HTTPS the same DNS message was sealed inside TLS, readable only by the resolver. The resolver still sees every question, so the trust moves to it, and the site you then visit can still be seen by its address. Press REPLAY to watch it again.
facts: The site’s address you then visit
Can’t be changed on the way

steps.title: Plain DNS
steps.desc: Readable by anyone on the way
steps.detail: This is the lookup from the other lessons: a UDP packet to port 53 asking for https://ssp-academy.com/, and the answer. Neither is encrypted, so everyone on the café’s Wi-Fi, and the internet provider, can see which names the laptop looks up, and could even answer with a false address.

steps.title: What Still Shows
steps.desc: Hidden on the way, not from the resolver
steps.detail: On the way, the lookups now look like any HTTPS traffic to dns.google. But the resolver itself reads every question, so you are trusting it instead of whoever runs your network. overview.description: Plain DNS answers can be forged: whoever answers first, or sits in the middle, can send a false address. DNSSEC lets a resolver check that an answer really comes from the domain’s owner. Every set of records is signed; each zone’s key is vouched for by its parent, up to the root, whose key resolvers have built in. DNSSEC proves answers are genuine; it doesn’t hide them.

outro.title: Answer checked
outro.desc: A chain of signatures to the root
outro.text: The resolver followed a chain: the address was signed by example.com’s key, that key by its key-signing key, which .com vouched for with a signed DS record, and .com’s key is vouched for by the root, whose key the resolver has built in. A forged answer would have broken the chain. Press REPLAY to watch it again.

overview.description: At home everyone shares one Wi-Fi password. Offices, universities and eduroam use WPA2- or WPA3-Enterprise instead: each person or device logs in with its own account or certificate, checked by a RADIUS server. The access point knows no passwords. It passes the login, a series of EAP messages, between the laptop and the server, and lets the laptop in only when the server says yes.

outro.title: Let in
outro.desc: Its own login, its own keys
outro.text: The laptop proved who it was with its certificate. The RADIUS server checked it and told the access point to let it in, on VLAN 20, with a key for this login alone. The access point never saw a password: it only passed the messages on. Press REPLAY to watch it again.

steps.title: Who Are You?
steps.desc: The access point asks for an identity
steps.detail: The laptop has joined “Office”, a WPA2-Enterprise network, but until it has logged in the access point passes on nothing except login messages. It asks who the laptop is with an EAP Identity request, and the laptop answers alex@example.org. The access point knows no accounts: it will pass the answer on to the RADIUS server.

steps.title: Why Enterprise
steps.detail: When someone leaves, their account is disabled and nobody else changes a password. Every login gets its own keys, so users can’t read each other’s traffic, and the RADIUS server records who connected and when. eduroam works the same way: a visitor’s login for user@their-university is passed from RADIUS server to RADIUS server until it reaches their own university.

overview.description: SMB is how Windows shares files and printers: \\server\share in File Explorer, a mapped network drive, a NAS at home. macOS and Linux speak it too. Over one TCP connection to port 445 the client agrees on a version, logs in and connects to a share, then opens, reads, writes and closes files with numbered requests.

outro.title: File read
outro.text: Over one TCP connection the laptop agreed on SMB 3.1.1, logged in with NTLM without sending its password, connected to the share and read a 240 KB file with a single request. Every message after the login was signed. Press REPLAY to watch it again.

steps.title: Port 445
steps.desc: A TCP connection to the NAS
steps.detail: The laptop opens \\nas\Documents, a shared folder on the NAS. It finds nas’s address with a local name lookup and opens a TCP connection to port 445. The packets pass through the home router to the NAS and never leave the home network.

steps.title: Negotiate
steps.detail: The laptop lists every SMB version it speaks, from 2.0.2 to 3.1.1, and says it requires signing. The NAS picks 3.1.1, the newest. Both sides keep a SHA-512 hash of everything exchanged from here until the login is done. It goes into the keys, so if anyone changed these messages on the way, to force an older version for instance, the login would fail.

steps.title: NTLM Challenge
steps.desc: The NAS sends a random number
steps.detail: A home NAS has no domain, so there is no Kerberos: the laptop logs in with NTLM. Its first SESSION_SETUP says it wants to log in, and the NAS answers “more processing required” with a challenge of 8 random bytes. It also gives this login a session ID.

steps.title: NTLM Response
steps.detail: The laptop answers with the user name, alex, and an NTLMv2 response: an HMAC of the challenge and a few other values, keyed with a hash of the password. The NAS has the same hash and works out the same value. The password itself never crosses the network, and both sides now have a session key to sign messages with.

steps.title: Close the File
steps.detail: CLOSE hands the file ID back; the connection stays open for the next file. SMB 3 can also encrypt every message with AES-GCM, for one share or a whole server. Here only signing protects the messages, so anyone on the network could read the file as it passed. Port 445 should never be reachable from the internet: the WannaCry worm (2017) spread through a flaw in the old SMB1.

overview.description: Modbus is one of the oldest and most widely used protocols in industrial control (OT, operational technology): PLCs, sensors, motor drives and meters in factories, water works and buildings speak it. A client reads and writes numbered registers and coils on a device. Modbus/TCP carries the same small messages over TCP port 502, with no login and no encryption.

outro.title: Pump running
outro.text: The laptop read four registers, changed a setpoint and started a pump, each with a 12-byte request and a short answer. No message carried a password and none was encrypted: Modbus trusts whoever can reach it, so the network around it has to do the protecting. Press REPLAY to watch it again.

steps.title: Port 502
steps.desc: A TCP connection to the PLC
steps.detail: A PLC (programmable logic controller) runs a small pumping station: it reads the sensors and switches the pumps. An engineer’s laptop on the plant network talks to it in Modbus/TCP, so it opens a TCP connection to port 502. In Modbus terms the laptop is the client and the PLC the server.

steps.title: Read Registers
steps.detail: The laptop asks for 4 holding registers starting at address 0, with function code 3. The PLC answers with 8 bytes: four 16-bit numbers. What they mean (the tank level in centimetres, the temperature in tenths of a degree) is written only in the PLC’s documentation; the message carries no names and no units. An HMI screen sends reads like this every second or so.

steps.title: Write a Setpoint
steps.detail: The engineer raises the tank’s level setpoint from 4.50 m to 5.00 m: function 6, write single register, register 3, value 500. The PLC answers by repeating the request, which means done. From now on its program keeps the tank fuller.

steps.title: Start a Pump
steps.detail: Coils are single on/off outputs. Function 5 writes one: coil 0, pump 2, value 0xFF00, which means on. The PLC switches the pump on and echoes the request. In a real plant the PLC’s own program usually decides this, with safety interlocks.

steps.title: No Security
steps.detail: Nothing in these messages says who sent them: Modbus, from 1979, has no login and no encryption, so any device that can reach port 502 can read the values and start the pump. Plants protect it with separate networks, firewalls between office and plant, lists of who may talk to each PLC, and monitoring. Modbus/TCP Security wraps the same messages in TLS, on port 802.

overview.description: The internet is a network of networks: tens of thousands of them, run by internet providers, clouds, universities and companies, each with its own AS number. BGP is how their border routers tell each other which addresses they can reach. Every router passes on what it learns with its own number added, so each network builds its own map of the paths to every address on the internet.

outro.title: Route learned
outro.text: The hosting network announced its addresses, the transit network passed them on with its own number added, and the ISP’s router used that path for the laptop’s packets. When the route was withdrawn, the news spread the same way. There is no central map: every network builds its own from what its neighbours say. Press REPLAY to watch it again.

steps.title: Many Networks
steps.detail: The internet is more than 75,000 separate networks, called autonomous systems (ASes): internet providers, clouds, universities, big companies, each with a number. Here are three: the laptop’s ISP (AS 64500), a transit network that carries others’ traffic (AS 64510), and the hosting network of https://ssp-academy.com/ (AS 64511). BGP is how their routers tell each other where every address can be reached.

steps.title: Open a Session
steps.detail: BGP routers don’t discover each other: engineers at both ends set each other up as neighbours. The ISP’s router opens a TCP connection to the transit router on port 179. They are directly connected, so their packets go out with a TTL of 1: they can’t cross even one more router, so the session only works between direct neighbours.

steps.title: Say Hello
steps.detail: Each router sends an OPEN: its AS number, a hold time of 180 seconds, its router ID and what it supports, such as 4-byte AS numbers. Each answers with a KEEPALIVE, and the session is established. From now on a KEEPALIVE goes every 60 seconds when there’s nothing else to send; after 180 silent seconds the session would be dropped.

steps.title: Passed On
steps.detail: The transit router accepts the route and passes it to its other neighbours, the ISP among them, with its own number added to the front: AS_PATH 64510 64511, and itself as the next hop. The ISP’s router may hear of the same prefix from several neighbours. It picks one by its own policy first (routes through paying customers before others, say), then by the shortest AS path.

steps.title: Follow the Route
steps.detail: When the laptop connects to https://ssp-academy.com/ (its address found by DNS as usual), its packets reach the ISP, whose router now sends anything for 203.0.113.0/24 to the transit router, and the transit router sends it on to the hosting network. The answer comes back by whatever route the hosting network chose towards the laptop’s ISP: on the internet the way back is often different from the way there.

steps.title: Withdrawn
steps.detail: Later the hosting network takes the prefix back, as it would if a link failed: an UPDATE listing it under withdrawn routes. The transit router passes it on, and within seconds to minutes networks everywhere forget the path. A session that goes quiet past its hold time loses all its routes at once. In 2021 Facebook withdrew the routes to its own DNS servers and vanished from the internet for six hours.

steps.title: Trust Problems
steps.detail: A router accepts what its neighbours announce. A network that announces addresses that aren’t its own, by mistake or on purpose, pulls their traffic towards it: in 2008 a Pakistani ISP took YouTube offline worldwide this way. With RPKI the holder of a prefix signs which AS may announce it, and routers that check drop any other. Filters on what each neighbour may announce do the rest.

overview.description: WebRTC lets two browsers call each other, with audio, video and data going straight between them, not through a server. A server only introduces them: they swap descriptions of what they can send and where they can be reached (signalling), find a way through both home routers with ICE and STUN, encrypt with DTLS, and send the media over UDP as SRTP.

outro.title: On the call
outro.desc: Introduced by a server, then direct
outro.text: The signalling server passed the offer and the answer between the two browsers, a STUN server told the laptop its public address, and an ICE check found a way through both home routers. After a DTLS handshake, encrypted audio and video went straight from one laptop to the other. Press REPLAY to watch it again.

steps.title: Join the Call
steps.detail: The laptop opens a call page on call.example.com, and the page keeps a WebSocket open to the server, inside TLS. It joins room 42, where Sam is already waiting. The server will pass messages between the two browsers. WebRTC doesn’t say how: every app does this signalling its own way.

steps.title: Public Address?
steps.detail: Behind its home router the laptop knows only its private address, 192.168.1.10, which nobody on the internet can reach. So it asks a STUN server named in the call page’s settings, with one small UDP request. The answer says where the request seemed to come from, 198.51.100.7 port 61022: the router’s public address and the port its NAT opened for this conversation.

steps.title: The Answer
steps.detail: Sam accepts the call. Sam’s browser answers with SDP of its own: the codecs it picked from the offer, its certificate fingerprint, its ICE user name and password, and its candidates, including its public address, 198.51.100.200 port 49170, which it learned from a STUN server the same way. It also says it will start the encryption handshake. Now each browser knows where the other might be reached.

steps.title: Punch Through
steps.detail: Now the browsers try pairs of addresses with STUN checks sent straight to each other (ICE). Each check also opens a way back through the sender’s own router, so once both sides have sent one, checks get through both NATs. This one is answered: the direct path works. The laptop then repeats the check with USE-CANDIDATE, choosing this pair for the call.

steps.title: DTLS Handshake
steps.detail: Over the same path the browsers run a DTLS handshake: TLS for UDP. Their certificates are self-signed, so each checks the other’s against the fingerprint in the SDP, which came through the signalling server inside TLS. The handshake also agrees the keys for SRTP, which encrypts the audio and video. WebRTC never sends media unencrypted.

steps.title: Media Flows
steps.detail: Audio goes in an SRTP packet every 20 ms, and video as frames split over several packets. Each packet has a readable RTP header (sequence number, timestamp, stream ID) and encrypted media. None of it passes through call.example.com. Both browsers watch delay and loss and adjust the video quality to suit, and a data channel for chat or files can share the same path.

steps.title: Peer to Peer
steps.detail: The server helped the two browsers find each other, then stepped aside: the call goes straight between the two homes. When a network won’t let direct packets through (some company firewalls, some mobile networks), ICE falls back to a TURN server that relays the encrypted media without being able to read it. Group calls usually send media through a server too, called an SFU.

overview.description: Ethernet carries almost every wired network, and Wi-Fi access points pass their traffic on to it. Every network card has a 48-bit MAC address. A frame says which card it is for and which card sent it, and a switch delivers it: it learns which port each address is behind from the frames it sees, and sends each frame only where it needs to go.

outro.title: Switched
outro.text: The switch learned where the laptop and the NAS were from the frames they sent, flooded only the broadcast, and sent every other frame out of just the port it needed. MAC addresses carried each frame across one link; at the router the packet moved into a new frame. Press REPLAY to watch it again.

steps.title: Who Has the NAS?
steps.desc: A broadcast asks for a MAC address
steps.detail: The laptop wants to reach the NAS at 192.168.1.20. On a local network, frames are delivered by MAC address, and the laptop doesn’t know the NAS’s yet. So it sends an ARP request to ff:ff:ff:ff:ff:ff, the broadcast address, into port 1 of the switch.

wire.at: Seen going into the switch, port 1

steps.title: Learn, Then Flood
steps.desc: The switch notes where the laptop is
steps.detail: A switch reads each frame’s source address and notes it in its MAC table: 00:00:5e:00:53:10 is on port 1. A broadcast is for everyone, so it sends a copy out of every other port: to the NAS on port 2 and the router on port 8. Frames for unknown addresses are flooded too.

steps.title: Only the NAS Answers
steps.desc: The reply goes to one port
steps.detail: Every device reads the request, but only the NAS has 192.168.1.20, so only it answers, straight to the laptop’s MAC; the router ignores it. The switch learns that 00:00:5e:00:53:20 is on port 2. It already knows where the laptop is, so the reply leaves by port 1 alone.

steps.title: Port to Port
steps.desc: Frames go only where they must
steps.detail: The laptop connects to the NAS. Each frame starts with the NAS’s MAC, then its own, then a type: 0x0800, an IPv4 packet. After the packet, the card adds a 4-byte checksum. The switch looks up the destination and sends each frame out of port 2 only. The router never sees them.

overview.description: Many DSL and fibre providers make the home router log in before it gets online. PPPoE is how: the router finds the provider’s access server and opens a session with it, then runs PPP inside, agreeing on the link’s settings, logging in with the username and password from the provider and receiving its public IP address. Every packet then carries an 8-byte PPPoE header.

outro.title: Logged in
outro.text: The router found the provider’s access server, got a session, agreed on the link’s settings, proved its password without sending it and was given its public address. Every packet now travels inside that session, until a PADT ends it. Press REPLAY to watch it again.

steps.title: Anyone There?
steps.desc: The router looks for an access server
steps.detail: The home router is plugged into the provider’s fibre or DSL line. Before it can log in, it has to find the provider’s access server, so it broadcasts a PADI: “PPPoE Active Discovery Initiation”. An access server answers with a PADO, an offer that names it: bng-1.example.net.

steps.title: Log In

overview.description: SIP sets up phone calls over the internet: office desk phones, phone apps and the providers behind them. A phone signs in with its provider’s SIP server. To call someone it sends an INVITE; the other phone rings and answers, and the two agree on how to send the voice, which then flows as RTP. The messages are plain text, a lot like HTTP.

outro.title: Call ended
outro.desc: Signed in, rang, talked, hung up
outro.text: Mohamed’s phone signed in with a password it never sent, invited Bob’s phone through the SIP server, heard it ring, and talked over RTP until Bob hung up with a BYE. SIP only set the call up and took it down; the voice travelled as packets of its own. Press REPLAY to watch it again.

steps.title: Sign In
steps.desc: The phone tells the server where it is
steps.detail: Mohamed’s phone, an app on her laptop, registers with her provider’s SIP server: mohamed@example.net can be reached here. The server answers 401 with a challenge, so the phone asks again with a hash made from the challenge and its password. 200 OK: registered for an hour.

overview.description: RTSP is how video players, recorders and security apps get live video from IP cameras. It works like a remote control: the player asks what the camera offers, sets up a stream, and says PLAY and later TEARDOWN, in text messages much like HTTP. The video itself doesn’t travel in RTSP: it flows separately as RTP, here over UDP.

outro.title: Watched
outro.text: VLC asked the camera what it had, logged in with a hash of its password, set up one video track and pressed PLAY. The video came as RTP packets on ports of its own, a key frame in three pieces, until TEARDOWN ended the session. Press REPLAY to watch it again.

steps.title: What Can You Do?

overview.description: Multicast sends one stream to a group address, and the network copies it only where it’s wanted: it’s how internet providers deliver live TV channels. IGMP is how a device tells its router which groups it wants. Switches listen in (IGMP snooping), so each stream reaches only the ports that asked for it.

outro.title: Tuned In
outro.text: The TV box and then the laptop joined channel 1 with IGMP reports. The router joined once for the whole home, and the switch, listening in, copied the channel only to the ports that wanted it. Queries kept it flowing, and when the laptop left, the TV box’s answer kept it on. Press REPLAY to watch it again.

steps.title: Pick a Channel
steps.desc: The TV box joins a group
steps.detail: The viewer picks channel 1. Each channel is a multicast group, here 233.252.0.1, and the TV box sends an IGMP Membership Report to that address: I want this group. The switch listens in (IGMP snooping), notes port 2, and passes the report to the router alone.

steps.title: Leave
steps.detail: Closing VLC sends a Leave Group to 224.0.0.2, all routers. Others may still watch, so the router asks about that group alone and waits 1 second. The TV box answers, so the channel stays; the switch just stops sending it to port 1.

overview.description: RTMP is how most streamers send live video to a platform: OBS and other apps push it to an ingest server, which turns it into streams for viewers. Made for Flash, it outlived Flash as the way to upload. Everything shares one TCP connection: commands, audio and video, cut into chunks.

outro.title: Live
outro.text: OBS shook hands with the ingest server, connected to its live app, got stream 1 and published to it with the stream key. The video and audio then flowed in chunks over the same TCP connection until the streamer stopped. Press REPLAY to watch it again.

steps.title: Handshake
steps.detail: The streamer clicks Start Streaming. OBS connects to the ingest server on TCP port 1935, then RTMP has its own handshake: version 3 and 1,536 random bytes each way, which each side sends back. It shows both ends speak RTMP; it encrypts nothing.
